title: Time Sync, Networking & Colocation
tagline: If you can't measure when things happened to the nanosecond, you can't trust your latency — or stay compliant.

concept.analogy: Imagine timing a sprint with everyone holding a different, slightly-wrong stopwatch. You'd never know who actually won. In trading, every machine, switch, and exchange has its own clock, and a millisecond of disagreement makes 'which order arrived first?' unanswerable and your latency numbers fiction. Time synchronization is getting every stopwatch agreeing to the nanosecond; the network and where you physically sit determine how fast the runners can even move.
paragraphs: Accurate, synchronized time underpins everything you've built. You need it to measure latency truthfully (a tick-to-trade number is meaningless if ingress and egress timestamps come from unsynced clocks), to sequence events across machines, to reconstruct exactly what happened during an incident, and to satisfy regulation: rules like MiFID II (RTS 25) and FINRA require business clocks synchronized to UTC within tight tolerances (microseconds for the fastest activity) with traceable, logged drift. Time is both an engineering tool and a compliance obligation.

The standards form a ladder of precision. NTP (Network Time Protocol) keeps machines within ~milliseconds — fine for general servers, far too coarse for HFT. PTP (Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588), especially with hardware timestamping in the NIC and PTP-aware switches (boundary/transparent clocks), reaches sub-microsecond to nanosecond accuracy. The reference is usually a GPS-disciplined grandmaster clock feeding PTP across the trading network, with NIC hardware clocks (PHC) disciplined to it. White Rabbit pushes this to sub-nanosecond for the most demanding setups.

On the wire itself, latency is dominated by physics and topology, not code. Propagation delay (~5 ns per meter in fiber, faster in air) means physical distance matters: this is why firms colocate their servers in the same data center as the exchange's matching engine and pay for short, equal-length cross-connect cables. Switching adds latency too, so HFT uses ultra-low-latency cut-through switches (forwarding a frame before it's fully received, vs store-and-forward) and minimizes hops. Between distant venues, microwave and laser links beat fiber because light travels faster through air than glass and takes a straighter path — a multi-millisecond edge that firms spend fortunes to capture.

Putting it together: a low-latency trading site has a GPS+PTP time hierarchy with hardware-timestamping NICs so every event is stamped to the nanosecond; cut-through switches and minimal hops; servers colocated at the exchange with tuned, often kernel-bypass, equal-length connectivity; and careful measurement of wire-to-wire latency using those hardware timestamps and external taps. The software you optimized in earlier lessons runs inside this physical envelope — and the envelope often dominates.
points: Synchronized time is needed for honest latency measurement, cross-machine sequencing, incident reconstruction, and regulatory compliance (MiFID II RTS 25 / FINRA).
Precision ladder: NTP (~ms, too coarse) → PTP/IEEE 1588 with HW timestamping + PTP switches (sub-µs to ns) → White Rabbit (sub-ns).
Reference is a GPS-disciplined grandmaster; NIC hardware clocks (PHC) are disciplined to it and stamp packets.
Wire latency is physics: ~5 ns/meter in fiber → colocate at the exchange, short/equal cross-connects, minimal hops.
Cut-through (not store-and-forward) switches; microwave/laser links beat fiber between distant venues.

callouts.title: Why microwave beats fiber
callouts.body: Light moves ~50% faster through air than through glass, and a microwave tower line is straighter than fiber routed along roads/rail. Over hundreds of kilometers (e.g., Chicago–New York) that's a multi-hundred-microsecond edge — worth enormous investment to the fastest firms.

callouts.title: Hardware timestamps are the truth
callouts.body: Software timestamps miss the NIC and switch and add jitter. NIC hardware timestamping (PHC, PTP) and external capture taps give the real wire-to-wire times you should trust for both measurement and compliance.

concept.keyIdea: Synchronized, nanosecond-accurate time (GPS-disciplined PTP with NIC hardware timestamping) makes latency measurable, events sequenceable, and trading compliant — while on the wire, physics rules: colocate at the exchange, use cut-through switches and minimal hops, and use microwave/laser between distant venues, because propagation and switching often dominate the latency your software runs inside.

deepDive.intro: The time hierarchy and how it's disciplined, hardware timestamping, low-latency networking, and colocation.

steps.title: The time hierarchy
steps.detail: A GPS receiver provides UTC traceability to a PTP grandmaster clock. PTP distributes time across the network: boundary/transparent clocks in switches correct for switch delay, and end hosts discipline their NIC hardware clock (PHC) and system clock to the grandmaster. PTP's hardware-timestamped exchange of sync/delay messages measures and removes path delay, achieving sub-microsecond (often tens of ns) accuracy versus NTP's milliseconds.

steps.title: Hardware timestamping
steps.detail: A capable NIC timestamps packets in hardware at the moment they cross the wire (PHC), independent of OS/software jitter. Use these to stamp market-data ingress and order egress, giving true wire-to-wire latency; tools like Linux's SO_TIMESTAMPING / hardware PTP and packet-capture appliances expose them. This is also the basis of compliant, traceable event timestamps.

steps.title: Low-latency switching
steps.detail: Store-and-forward switches receive a whole frame before forwarding (latency scales with frame size); cut-through switches start forwarding once they've read the header (fixed, tiny latency). HFT uses cut-through, ultra-low-latency switches, minimizes the number of hops, and sometimes uses layer-1 (physical-layer) switches/replicators that add only nanoseconds for fan-out of market data.

steps.title: Colocation and cross-connects
steps.detail: Because propagation is ~5 ns/m in fiber, firms place servers in the exchange's data center (colocation) and buy direct cross-connects to the matching engine and feeds. Exchanges often equalize cable lengths so no colo cabinet has a distance advantage. Within the cabinet, you minimize cable length and hops and use the fastest NIC/switch gear.

steps.title: Long-haul: microwave & lasers
steps.detail: Between geographically separate venues, signal speed and path straightness matter. Microwave and millimeter-wave/laser links carry data through air (faster than glass) on near-straight tower-to-tower paths, beating fiber by hundreds of microseconds over long distances — at the cost of lower bandwidth and weather sensitivity, so they carry only the most latency-critical signals with fiber as backup.

notes.title: Measure clock quality
notes.detail: PTP isn't fire-and-forget: monitor offset and drift continuously (and log it for compliance). A clock that has silently drifted makes your latency stats and audit trail wrong.

notes.title: Sequence first, time second
notes.detail: For ordering events from one source, sequence numbers are authoritative; timestamps are for cross-source correlation and measurement. Use both — don't infer order purely from possibly-imperfect clocks.

notes.title: It's mostly physics at the top
notes.detail: Once your software is in the tens-of-ns range, further wins often come from the network and location, not code. Know where the dominant latency actually is before optimizing.

complexity.timeReason: Hardware timestamping plus PTP path-delay correction removes software jitter and network asymmetry, taking accuracy from NTP's milliseconds to PTP's sub-microsecond/nanosecond range.
complexity.spaceReason: The cost here is hardware and topology — grandmaster clocks, capable NICs/switches, colocation — not application memory.

pitfalls: Using NTP-level (millisecond) time for HFT measurement or compliance — far too coarse.
Trusting software timestamps for wire latency, ignoring NIC/switch contributions and OS jitter.
Not monitoring/logging PTP offset & drift, so a silently bad clock corrupts stats and the audit trail.
Optimizing code while the real latency lives in extra switch hops, store-and-forward gear, or distance.
Inferring event order from clocks across sources instead of using authoritative sequence numbers.

interviewQuestions.q: Why does an HFT firm need nanosecond-level time synchronization, and how is it achieved?
a: Reasons: you can't measure latency honestly if ingress and egress timestamps come from clocks that disagree; you need a common time to sequence and correlate events across machines and reconstruct incidents; and regulation requires it — MiFID II RTS 25 and FINRA mandate business clocks synchronized to UTC within tight tolerances (microseconds for HFT) with traceable, logged drift.

How: a GPS receiver gives UTC-traceable time to a PTP (IEEE 1588) grandmaster clock; PTP distributes it across the network with boundary/transparent clocks in switches correcting for switch delay, and end hosts discipline their NIC hardware clock (PHC) to it. With hardware timestamping in the NIC, packets are stamped at the wire independent of software jitter, achieving sub-microsecond to nanosecond accuracy — versus NTP's milliseconds, which is far too coarse. The clock offset/drift is monitored and logged continuously for compliance.

interviewQuestions.q: Once the software is fast, where does the remaining tick-to-trade latency come from, and what do firms do about it?
a: It comes from physics and topology: propagation delay (~5 ns per meter in fiber), switching latency, and the number of network hops — the wire, not the code. Over distance this dominates; even within a building, extra hops and store-and-forward switches add up.

Firms attack it physically: colocate servers in the exchange's data center with direct, often length-equalized cross-connects to the matching engine; use ultra-low-latency cut-through switches (which forward after reading the header rather than the whole frame) and minimize hops, sometimes with layer-1 replicators for market-data fan-out; and between distant venues use microwave/laser links that travel through air (faster than glass) on straighter paths, beating fiber by hundreds of microseconds. The principle is to know where the dominant latency actually is — frequently it's location and network, so the highest-leverage 'optimization' is physical, not in the code.

problems.title: Design trustworthy latency measurement across the stack
problems.statement: You must report compliant, trustworthy wire-to-wire tick-to-trade latency for a colocated trading system and prove your clocks are accurate. Describe the time hierarchy you'd deploy, where and how you'd timestamp, how you'd compute the latency, and how you'd demonstrate clock accuracy/traceability to an auditor. Note the failure modes you'd monitor.
problems.hint: GPS→PTP grandmaster→PTP switches→NIC PHC; hardware-timestamp ingress (market data) and egress (order); subtract; log PTP offset/drift; monitor for drift and asymmetry.

approach: Time hierarchy: deploy a GPS-disciplined PTP grandmaster (UTC-traceable) feeding PTP (IEEE 1588) across PTP-aware switches (boundary/transparent clocks to correct switch delay); each trading host disciplines its NIC hardware clock (PHC) and system clock to the grandmaster. This gives sub-microsecond/nanosecond, traceable time.

Timestamping & computation: hardware-timestamp the market-data packet at NIC ingress (the event that triggers a decision) and hardware-timestamp the resulting order at NIC egress, both via the PHC. Wire-to-wire tick-to-trade = egress_ts − ingress_ts; record into per-stage and end-to-end HdrHistograms and report p50/p99/p99.9/max. Cross-check with an external packet-capture tap that independently timestamps both packets, so measurement doesn't depend solely on the host.

Proving accuracy to an auditor: continuously log the PTP offset and drift of each clock versus the GPS-traceable grandmaster, retain those logs, and show the synchronization stays within the required tolerance (e.g., MiFID II RTS 25 limits) with UTC traceability through GPS. Provide the time-source documentation and the monitored offset history as evidence.

Failure modes to monitor and alert on: PTP grandmaster loss or GPS holdover, clock offset/drift exceeding tolerance, path asymmetry or a misbehaving (non-PTP) switch inflating error, PHC vs system-clock divergence, and capture-tap vs host-timestamp disagreement. If the clock falls out of tolerance, flag affected measurements as untrusted and (for compliance) record the gap.

complexity.time: Sub-µs/ns clock accuracy; O(1) per-event stamp
